strengths: The topic of explaining foraging behavior in real-world environments is both intriguing and relevant, contributing to the understanding of animal behavior.
The paper strives to bridge the gap between computational and implementational aspects of behavior, providing a comprehensive view.
The use of a real-world dataset to validate the proposed methodology adds value to the research, demonstrating its practical applicability.
Refreshing and interesting read about social bird foraging behaviors, their individual differences, and general background.
Appealingly simple models of individual species behavior.
The paper shows that the inference of simple behavioral patterns is possible – at least on the simple level parameters are identifiable.

The goal of the paper is highly important and interesting to the computational neuroscience community. While foraging has been an objective of studies since the 70s, recently its focus has moved from lab experiments to (more) naturalistic behaviors of (groups of) animals interacting in the wild (or almost wild) conditions. In that regard, a computational framework to analyze data from such experiments is timely.

The Authors in this paper aimed to build a unified framework spanning several levels of analysis (i.e., cognitive, network, and algorithmic levels), which, I think, is especially important in the field of foraging because conventionally different levels of analysis were treated separately in the field.

The paper describes a new dataset and lays out the plans to collect more data using an even better technology. This is doubly valuable because new data will allow these and other researchers to test their models of foraging, and also, should additional data be needed to test new hypotheses, the Authors do have a set up framework in place to record such data.

The research is perfectly structured starting with the framework that unifies different levels of analysis, then using synthetic data to validate the framework, later applying the framework to existing data and reproducing the findings in a principled manner, and, finally, introducing new data and obtaining new knowledge off of it.
The application of the statistical model to real-world data is interesting, and seems to provide some information.
Basically, the scientific content, as far as I managed to understand it, seems interesting and potentially valuable.
weaknesses: The main point of the paper is difficult to grasp; proposals, models, and their relations are unclear, and experiments only show relevance of the cognitive model without concrete evidence that the neural implementation is necessary.
Section 2.2.2 is unclear about whether a model is proposed and simulated or quantities are inferred; the role of Bayesian inference is not clearly explained.

The sentence about birds updating their expected reward vector is ambiguous, leaving it unclear whether some birds are modeled differently or the behavior emerges from uniformly modeled birds; clearer statements of what was done are needed.
Formulations such as "When animals decide what action to take, they sample their local environment" are questionable in terms of representing actual mechanisms in real animals.

The paper does not really have anything novel to offer – or this novelty is at the moment fully hidden; it merely reports how to generally model multi-agent foraging behavior with very simple techniques, lacking true novelty.
The paper provides no insights into which model may work better for social foraging; there are no ablations or comparisons to existing baselines, making the contribution difficult to assess.

The utility of the presented results is minor; figures report performance on simulated data, parameter identifiability is unsurprising, and results are summarized but not interpreted, lacking deeper understanding of foraging behavior.

Results in 2.3.1 infer locust communication about food locations without offering interesting insights; a more detailed analysis of the locust data could better demonstrate the model's ability to uncover communication patterns.

Results in 2.3.2 report that ducks and small songbirds keep distances, which is hardly surprising and could be measured with a simple summary statistic; lack of comparison makes it unclear whether modeling individual foraging decisions is useful, and Figure 4 lacks clear labeling and explanation of posterior distributions.
Evaluations do not convincingly show what the model can demonstrate, especially relative to other models; ablation studies or baseline comparisons are needed to judge model quality.
Key techniques used – whether novel or merely important for modeling foraging behavior – remain fully obscured.
No direct links or mapping onto the brain at the network level; the paper lacks a mapping of the proposed weight matrices to brain structures, limiting biological relevance.

Handcrafted features ("proximity", "trace") and handcrafted classes ("random", "hungry", "follower") may mismatch animal behavior and may be insufficiently expressive; a low‑dimensional representation and unsupervised clustering could be more appropriate.

Communication is modeled as a single scalar 0‑1, ignoring different content signals (e.g., food location vs. quantity) and species‑specific reliance; analyzing content of messages could strengthen results.
The paper is clearly unpolished and unfinished; the description is extremely confusing and incomplete, making it hard to understand and replicate the method.

Explanation of various parts of the method is split across the main text and the Appendix; authors do not define what they call a "cognitive", "neural" or "statistical" model until page 4, hindering comprehension.

The introduction and discussion are overly lengthy and philosophical, figures are absurdly small, and the methods description is inadequate or missing; most basic explanations are pushed to the Appendix and remain insufficient for reproduction.
Unclear definition of predictors (e.g., f_i); the paper lacks a clear definition of their functional form, whether they are fixed or learned, making the statistical model difficult to assess.

Successor representation is described as "Discounted expected occupancy" but is actually based on the iterated transition matrix, effectively a distance function; the paper does not clarify the implications of using a random‑walk policy for the SR and its impact on goal‑directed behavior.

In the neural model it is unclear whether the matrix M is specified by hand or learned; insufficient detail on how the successor representation is implemented in the neural network hampers assessment of biological plausibility.
The statistical model is only described in the Appendix inadequately; core components such as predictors and coefficients are not introduced in the main text, making the results incomprehensible.
The paper fails to distinguish between parameters that are fit to data and those that are hand‑specified, making it difficult to evaluate the model's ability to generalize to new data.
Simulation details of "hungry, follower and random" birds are relegated to the Appendix and not properly introduced in the main text, obscuring the experimental setup.
Description of the proximity function is vague; the combination of two sine waves and an exponential is not mathematically formulated, hindering replication.
In 2.2.2 the reported estimated parameter values lack the true values, leaving unclear whether zero effects are true in the simulation.
"Maximum projection of thermal images" is not clearly defined, and the paper provides insufficient context for this data processing step.

Figure 4 uses a cumbersome way to recover the underlying proximity‑preference function; a different parametrization (e.g., polynomial times decaying exponential) could achieve the same goal more efficiently.
Figure labeling is insufficient; subplots need letters and explicit references in captions to improve readability.
